summary: Specifies new SNMP textual conventions for additional high capacity data types, intended for implementations that already support the Counter64 data type. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some counters grow so large that the old ones overflow. This defines a few more kinds of big counters for network management.

questions: why is there no gauge64 in snmp
subtitle: Two stopgap SNMP data types for unsigned 64-bit values, built on top of Counter64.

tldr.problem: SMIv2 has no 64-bit gauge or other unsigned 64-bit type besides the Counter64 counter, yet new MIBs need to store snapshots and differences of Counter64 values and zero-based 64-bit counters.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two textual conventions, CounterBasedGauge64 and ZeroBasedCounter64, that reuse the Counter64 syntax and its ASN.1 encoding but give the value gauge-like or zero-start semantics.
tldr.outcome: They are explicitly a short-term solution that may be deprecated once a proper base type is defined and deployed.

today: RFC 2856 is a Proposed Standard with no recorded obsoleting or updating RFC. Its own text says the textual conventions are a short-term solution that may be deprecated once a long-term replacement is defined and deployed.

sections.title: Where This Fits in SNMP
sections.content:
RFC 2856 is a small MIB module that defines no management objects of its own. It defines textual conventions (TCs): named types that other MIB modules can use for their objects. The module is compliant to SMIv2, the second version of the Structure of Management Information.

Because the new types rely on the Counter64 type, which does not exist in SMIv1, the textual conventions cannot be translated to SMIv1.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a box of labelled stickers. The memo does not measure anything itself. It only makes two new stickers that other people can put on their own measurements.

sections.title: The Missing 64-bit Types
sections.content:
The SMI does not say how to represent integer objects, other than counters, that need up to 64 bits of range and precision. Some MIBs in progress for the standards track needed such types, so the RFC offers a short-term fix.

There is an immediate need for a Gauge64 type, similar to Gauge32, to hold a snapshot of a Counter64 at a given moment (for example a history ring buffer) or the difference between two Counter64 values. There is also a need for a 64-bit zero-based counter like the ZeroBasedCounter32 TC in the RMON-2 MIB (RFC 2021).

Ideally both would use a base type of Gauge64 or Unsigned64, but no such base type is available. Until one is defined and deployed, the temporary TCs use a base type of Counter64.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a counter that can hold huge numbers, but no gauge that can hold huge numbers. Until someone builds one, people borrow the counter's container.

sections.title: CounterBasedGauge64
sections.content:
CounterBasedGauge64 is a 64-bit gauge declared with Counter64 syntax. It is used to store the difference between two Counter64 values, or a snapshot of a Counter64 at a given moment.

Its value is a non-negative integer that may increase or decrease but never exceeds a maximum value or falls below a minimum value. The maximum cannot be greater than 2^64-1 (18446744073709551615 decimal) and the minimum cannot be smaller than 0. The value sits at the maximum whenever the modelled information is at or above it, and at the minimum whenever the information is at or below it.

The RFC admits this TC is not strictly supported in SMIv2, because the "always increasing" and "counter wrap" semantics of Counter64 are not preserved. A management application that decides semantics only from the Counter64 ASN.1 tag may wrongly treat such objects like ordinary counters.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a gauge like a fuel needle: it can go up or down, but it stops at the top and bottom of the dial instead of wrapping around.

sections.title: ZeroBasedCounter64
sections.content:
ZeroBasedCounter64 is a 64-bit counter with an initial value of zero, instead of an arbitrary initial value. Objects of this type are set to zero on creation, then count events, wrapping back to zero when the value 2^64 is reached. It is used for counters in tables whose rows are instantiated by management application action.

If an application discovers a new object within the minimum time to wrap, it can treat the initial value as a delta since it last polled the table. The management station has to know that minimum time and the actual time between polls, and discard data if the actual time is too long or there is no defined minimum time.

Typically this TC is used in tables where the INDEX space is constantly changing, or where the TimeFilter mechanism is in use. A plain Counter64 starts at an arbitrary value, so this TC drops that part of the Counter64 semantics. The RFC says this is not likely to harm management applications that expect Counter64 semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal counter might start at any number when you first see it. This one always starts at zero, like a fresh stopwatch, so the first number you read tells you how much happened since it began.

sections.title: Encoding and Limitations
sections.content:
To stay backward compatible with existing Counter64 implementations, the ASN.1 encoding of these unsigned 64-bit types must be identical to Counter64, identified by the [APPLICATION 6] ASN.1 tag. Reusing the Counter64 tag brings four limitations:

  • The MAX-ACCESS of the TC must be read-only, because that of Counter64 is read-only.
  • No sub-range can be specified, because sub-ranges are not allowed on Counter64 objects.
  • No DEFVAL clause can be specified, because DEFVALs are not allowed on Counter64 objects.
  • The TC-derived types cannot be used in an INDEX clause, because no INDEX mapping is defined for Counter64.

The module itself is HCNUM-TC, registered under mib-2 78, with the identity hcnumTC.
sections.plainLanguage: The new types wear the old counter's uniform, so old software still recognizes them. The price is that they also have to follow the old counter's rules, such as being read-only.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The module defines no management objects, only textual conventions that other MIB modules may use to define objects. The RFC therefore says that meaningful security considerations can only be written in the modules that define the management objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A sticker cannot be dangerous by itself. Whatever is risky lives in the things the stickers are put on.
